Hi all, I’m Peter Chen.

I was graduated from University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign about 10 years ago.

My recent merged work has mostly been around correctness, regression testing, and performance: API and MCP pagination semantics in Langfuse, RPC correctness fixes in Nethermind, compiler-lowering work in fractalyze, and MSM benchmarking in Aztec’s Barretenberg stack.

I’m now trying to go deeper on Lean, formalization, and proof engineering. I’ve started reading through FLT and related discussions, and I with to learn and contribute here. If there are good entry points for someone coming from systems, compiler, and performance work, I’d be glad to hear about them.

This isn't normally recommended for beginners, but given your background in compilers you'll probably be interested in metaprogramming in lean (there's a book here: https://leanprover-community.github.io/lean4-metaprogramming-book/ although it requires functional programming in lean as a prerequisite). Basically, all part's of Lean's compilation pipeline can be hooked into and modified at any point. People have used this to add all sorts of new features to the language. If you intend to eventually contribute to Lean's compiler, you'll probably want to start here.

For distributed systems, Lean and mathlib are getting to the point where they require all sorts of custom infrastructure to be built to support their scaling. Most of this work is probably not that accessible right now, but it might be worth asking around.

For software verification, you should probably check out the iris, aeneas, and mvcgen frameworks, as these each do verification in a different way.

For proofs, you'll want to learn starting with #tpil (bottom-up approach) or #mil (top down approach, aimed towards people with a background in undergraduate math). I'm not sure what you mean by proof engineering; do you want to write proofs in Lean or did you mean something else?

If you intend to eventually contribute to Lean's compiler, you'll probably want to start here.

I mean proof engineering in the broader sense: building useful proof infrastructure, automation, metaprogramming, compiler-facing tooling, and fixing awkward edges in the workflow, not just writing standalone proofs.

If you have a concrete first task that would stress those skills, please send it my way. I’d rather prove myself on a real problem than speculate in the abstract.
Take a look at #iris-lean. Iris has a separate proof mode build on top of Lean that allows you to write separation logic proofs. And the Iris proof mode still needs a lot of work.
